extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legislators, and educated readers of political economy
extracted.subtask_short: state policy on education and religion
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for government institutions and public policy concerning popular education, military training, clergy provision, and the management of religious sects and public morals. Focuses on what the state should do (or avoid) to promote useful instruction, public order, and civic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public facilitation of essential education for the common people
rubrics_metrics.description: The most essential parts of education, however, to read, write, and account, can be acquired at so early a period of life, that the greater part, even of those who are to be bred to the lowest occupations, have time to acquire them before they can be employed in those occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public can facilitate this acquisition by establishing in every parish or district a little school, where children maybe taught for a reward so moderate, that even a common labourer may afford it; the master being partly, but not wholly, paid by the public; because, if he was wholly, or even principally, paid by it, he would soon learn to neglect his business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of parish/district schools and funding mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish in every parish or district a little school with a moderate reward; the master should be partly, but not wholly, paid by the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the master were wholly or principally paid by the public he would soon learn to neglect his business. In Scotland parish schools taught almost the whole common people to read, and in England charity schools had similar though less universal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical curriculum for the common people (geometry/mechanics over Latin)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, instead of a little smattering in Latin ... they were instructed in the elementary parts of geometry and mechanics; the literary education of this rank of people would, perhaps, be as complete as can be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is scarce a common trade which does not afford some opportunities of applying to it the principles of geometry and mechanics, and which would not, therefore, gradually exercise and improve the common people in those principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of small premiums and badges to encourage learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The public can encourage the acquisition of those most essential parts of education, by giving small premiums, and little badges of distinction, to the children of the common people who excel in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small rewards and public marks of distinction can stimulate effort among children who otherwise might not have incentive to pursue basic literacy and numeracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory examination/probation before trade or corporate freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The public can impose upon almost the whole body of the people the necessity of acquiring the most essential parts of education, by obliging every man to undergo an examination or probation in them, before he can obtain the freedom in any corporation, or be allowed to set up any trade, either in a village or town corporate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring proof of basic instruction as a condition of entering trades or obtaining corporate freedom forces near-universal acquisition of essential skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: State facilitation of military and gymnastic exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: They facilitated the acquisition of those exercises, by appointing a certain place for learning and practising them, and by granting to certain masters the privilege of teaching in that place. Those masters do not appear to have had either salaries or exclusive privileges of any kind. Their reward consisted altogether in what they got from their scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public places (gymnasia) and non-salaried masters supported by pupils foster widespread martial skill without creating entrenched public dependents; a citizen trained publicly had no legal advantage over one trained privately, provided equal proficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, universal institutions for keeping martial spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient institutions of Greece and Rome seem to have been much more effectual for maintaining the martial spirit of the great body of the people, than the establishment of what are called the militias of modern times. They were much more simple. When they were once established, they executed themselves, and it required little or no attention from government to maintain them in the most perfect vigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex modern militia regulations require continual and painful government attention and tend to fall into neglect; simplicity and universality sustain martial habits more reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate martial spirit to reduce standing army dependence and domestic danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Where every citizen had the spirit of a soldier, a smaller standing army would surely be requisite. That spirit, besides, would necessarily diminish very much the dangers to liberty, whether real or imaginary, which are commonly apprehended from a standing army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martial spirit among the populace both aids defence against foreign invaders and obstructs potential domestic misuse of a standing army against the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: State should alter conduct toward callings that bring no private advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: There are also some callings which, though useful and even necessary in a state, bring no advantage or pleasure to any individual; and the supreme power is obliged to alter its conduct with regard to the retainers of those professions. It must give them public encouragement in order to their subsistence; and it must provide against that negligence to which they will naturally be subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For such professions (e.g., persons employed in the finances, fleets, and magistracy) the state must provide public encouragement, honours, long subordination of ranks, strict dependence, or other expedients to secure diligence and subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off in clergy remuneration and effects on zeal and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The teachers of the doctrine ... may either depend altogether for their subsistence upon the voluntary contributions of their hearers; or they may derive it from some other fund ... Their exertion, their zeal and industry, are likely to be much greater in the former situation than in the latter. ... But if we consider the matter more closely, we shall find that this interested diligence of the clergy is what every wise legislator will study to prevent; because, in every religion except the true, it is highly pernicious, and it has even a natural tendency to pervert the truth, by infusing into it a strong mixture of superstition, folly, and delusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary dependence tends to greater industry and popular appeal but also incentivizes exploitation of passions and superstition; salaried, endowed clergy may become learned and genteel but lose popular influence. The state must weigh zeal and popular influence against risks of superstition and perversion of doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public provision (salaries) can 'bribe indolence' but stabilize clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: And in this manner ecclesiastical establishments, though commonly they arose at first from religious views, prove in the end advantageous to the political interests of society. ... the most decent and advantageous composition, which he can make with the spiritual guides, is to bribe their indolence, by assigning stated salaries to their profession, and rendering it superfluous for them to be farther active, than merely to prevent their flock from straying in quest of new pastors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning stated salaries reduces incentives for frantic proselytizing and fanaticism, trading off some popular vigour for political stability and reduced social disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid state establishment of a single religion; favor legal equality among sects
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country where the law favoured the teachers of no one religion more than those of another, it would not be necessary that any of them should have any particular or immediate dependency upon the sovereign or executive power; or that he should have anything to do either in appointing or in dismissing them from their offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal neutrality prevents the sovereign from needing to influence teachers and reduces the clerical incorporation that can act against the sovereign; equality of treatment encourages multiplicity of small sects and reduces danger from any single powerful religious corporation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage multiplicity of small sects to foster candour and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: The teachers of each little sect, seeing themselves surrounded on all sides with more adversaries than friends, would be obliged to learn that candour and moderation which are so seldom to be found among the teachers of those great sects ... The concessions which they would mutually find it both convenient and agreeable to make one to another, might in time, probably reduce the doctrine of the greater part of them to that pure and rational religion, free from every mixture of absurdity, imposture, or fanaticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous small sects competing and coexisting produce incentives for moderation, mutual respect, and doctrinal refinement; large established sects are likelier to be intolerant and political.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two remedies to cure unsocial rigor among sects: science and public diversions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two very easy and effectual remedies ... The first ... the study of science and philosophy, which the state might render almost universal among all people of middling or more than middling rank and fortune ... The second ... the frequency and gaiety of public diversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Institute probations and requirements to study higher sciences for those entering liberal professions or candidacy for offices to secure learning among superior ranks. 2) Encourage arts, painting, poetry, music, dancing, drama and other diversions (allowed so long as not scandalous or indecent) to dissipate melancholy and the temper favorable to superstition; dramatic representations especially expose fanatic arts to ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of political parties granting independent provision to clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Times of violent religious controversy have generally been times of equally violent political faction. Upon such occasions, each political party has either found it, or imagined it, for his interest, to league itself with some one or other of the contending religious sects. ... Their first demand was generally that he should silence and subdue all their adversaries, and their second, that he should bestow an independent provision on themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When political winners favor a sect, that sect will seek legal advantages and independent provision; the state should be wary because this creates entrenched clergy who can overawe the civil magistrate and demand protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established clergy act as an incorporated body with collective political interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The clergy of every established church constitute a great incorporation. They can act in concert, and pursue their interest upon one plan, and with one spirit as much as if they were under the direction of one man; and they are frequently, too, under such direction. Their interest as an incorporated body is never the same with that of the sovereign, and is sometimes directly opposite to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a church creates a corporate clergy able to coordinate and pursue interests potentially at odds with the sovereign; this is a political risk to be considered in formation or maintenance of ecclesiastical establishments.
